data.name: Puerto Rico
data.summary: Ordinary Puerto Rico residents pay 15% on long-term gains and dividends, and there is no local estate, gift or wealth tax. The draw is the Act 60 resident investor decree: 0% on dividends, interest and post-move gains until 2035 for applications filed by 31 Dec 2026; Act 38-2026 sets 4% until 2055 for later applicants. For US citizens, federal income tax still reaches non-Puerto Rico-source income such as foreign dividends, and US federal estate and gift tax still applies.

regimes.name: Ordinary tax residence (no decree)
regimes.description: Residents are taxed on worldwide income. Long-term capital gains 15%, dividends 15%, progressive rates up to 33% plus a 5% surtax above USD 500,000 on other income.
regimes.eligibility: Domicile in Puerto Rico; presence of 180+ days creates a presumption of residence. Non-US citizens need US immigration status to live in Puerto Rico.

capital_gains.summary: Long-term capital gains (assets held over one year) are taxed at a special 15% rate; short-term gains at ordinary rates up to 33%.

regimes.name: Act 60 Individual Resident Investor (application filed by 31 Dec 2026)
regimes.description: Decree under Chapter 2 of Act 60-2019 (ex Act 22): 0% Puerto Rico tax on interest, dividends and on capital gains accrued after becoming resident, until 31 Dec 2035. Pre-move gains: 5% if recognised 10+ years after moving, otherwise ordinary rules.
regimes.eligibility: Application must reach DDEC by 31 Dec 2026, 11:59 pm. Applicant must not have been a Puerto Rico resident between 17 Jan 2006 and 17 Jan 2012. Buy a primary residence in Puerto Rico within two years of the decree. Annual USD 10,000 donation to Puerto Rico nonprofits, annual report and fees. Background check. Must become a bona fide Puerto Rico resident.

capital_gains.summary: Post-move capital gains: 0% Puerto Rico tax until 31 Dec 2035. Appreciation accrued before the move: 5% if recognised after 10 years of residence (by 2035), otherwise taxed under the normal rules (15%).
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Pre-residency built-in gains are not exempt (5% after 10 years, otherwise 15%).

data.us_citizen_notes: Puerto Rico is the one place where a US citizen can reduce US federal income tax by moving. A bona fide Puerto Rico resident excludes Puerto Rico-source income from US gross income (IRC §933). Gains on securities sold by a bona fide resident are generally Puerto Rico-source for appreciation after the move (IRC §865/§937 regulations; gains accrued in the 10 years before the move are treated as US-source - not re-verified here). Dividends and interest from US or foreign companies are NOT Puerto Rico-source, so they remain fully US-taxed even with an Act 60 decree. US federal estate and gift tax continues to apply to mainland-born US citizens: IRC §2209 treats a possession resident as a non-citizen only if citizenship came solely from the possession. The IRS has an active compliance campaign on Act 60 residency claims.
open_questions: FOMB endorsement status of Act 38-2026: no Board letter or statement on the Act found in its documents library (checked 2026-10-15); DDEC applies it as in force.
Tax position of non-US citizens (EU/OTHER) living in Puerto Rico under US immigration status (green card makes them US tax residents) not modelled; Act 60 is designed for US citizens.
Source rules for pre-move gains (IRC §937 regulations) not re-verified in this pass.

Family rent (USD 5,235) is an island-wide condo/townhouse average and was not replaced: only individual Dorado/Guaynabo 4-bedroom houses were seen in search results (USD 3,600-4,900 in Dorado del Mar/Paseo del Mar, USD 4,200 in Mansiones Reales, USD 9,500 in Garden Hills Estates), and Zillow, Trulia, Realtor, RentHop and Maxlife pages returned 403 or were off the market, so no median of several current listings could be opened; it may understate a Garden Hills/Dorado family house.

income.name: Puerto Rico

income_tax.summary: Progressive Puerto Rico income tax of 0% to USD 9,000, then 7%, 14%, 25% and 33% above USD 61,500, with the total tax equal to 95% of the computed amount (92% for gross income up to USD 100,000). Employees pay US FICA of 7.65% (self-employed 15.3%).
income_tax.self_employed_notes: Deloitte gives the employee shares: OASDI 6.2% on wages up to USD 184,500 (2026) and Medicare 1.45% on all wages; the cap applies to the OASDI part only. The self-employed pay both shares: 12.4% + 2.9% = 15.3% (summed from Deloitte's employee and employer figures; the page does not state the self-employment rate directly).
income_tax.local_tax_note: Brackets are the nominal Puerto Rico schedule; the first USD 9,000 band reflects the personal exemption. The total tax is 95% of the regular tax (92% when gross income is up to USD 100,000), so the effective top marginal rate at USD 150,000 is about 31.35%; a 5% surtax applies above USD 500,000 of net taxable income and an alternate basic tax may apply. Residents are taxed on worldwide income; long-term capital gains 15%. No municipal income tax. The 95%/92% adjustment is not folded into the brackets.

open_questions: The 95%/92% adjustment factor is described by Deloitte as 'total tax equals 95% of the regular tax plus the surtax (92% for gross income up to USD 100,000)'; how it interacts with deductions and credits (and the alternate basic tax) was not researched, and it is not folded into the brackets (it lowers the modelled tax by 5% to 8%).
US citizens living in Puerto Rico also owe US federal tax on non-Puerto Rico-source income, and self-employment tax; see regimes.

Puerto Rico: social_security_deductible left null. The PR Internal Revenue Code (OGP text rev. 18 June 2026) lets an individual in trade or business deduct 50% of the federal self-employment tax (s. 1033.01(b)(3)), but no clear deduction for employee FICA was found in s. 1033.15(a); (a)(6) covers government retirement systems only, and the Hacienda booklet is silent. Employee FICA is likely not deductible (0) and half of SE tax is for the self-employed.

regimes.name: Act 60 export services decree (4% fixed rate)
regimes.description: A decree under Act 60-2019 (Chapter 3, export services) gives an operating business a 4% Puerto Rico income tax rate on eligible income from services performed in Puerto Rico for clients outside Puerto Rico (consulting, technology, marketing, R&D, financial and management services), with dividends from decree income to Puerto Rico resident owners exempt. The DDEC's Incentives Code brochure lists 'Export of services or goods from Puerto Rico to foreign markets' with a '4% income tax rate' and 100% income tax exemption on dividends; InCorp states the services must be performed in Puerto Rico for clients located outside it. The relief is therefore for work done while living and operating in Puerto Rico (covers_local_work true). It is granted to a business (often a one-person company), needs a bona fide office and substance, and does not change a salary earned as an ordinary employee.
regimes.duration_note: Decree term 15 years, renewable for another 15 if in compliance (InCorp). A 2% rate for the first five years for businesses with annual volume up to USD 3 million is also reported by InCorp but not verified.

US citizens: a bona fide Puerto Rico resident (IRC 933 / 937 tests) generally excludes Puerto Rico-source income from US federal income tax, but self-employment tax (15.3%) still applies and US-source income, dividends and interest stay US-taxable. Green card holders are US taxpayers; EU and other non-US citizens need US immigration status to work in Puerto Rico. The IRS scrutinises residency claims.

income.residence_routes: US citizens can move freely and work. Citizens of the EU and other countries need US immigration status (visa or green card) because Puerto Rico follows US immigration law; there is no remote-worker visa and no nomad tax regime. Act 60 does not give immigration rights. Act 60 export services decrees (4%) are for businesses serving clients outside Puerto Rico; the separate Individual Resident Investor decree concerns investment income, not earned income. US citizenship interaction: a US citizen who becomes a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico (presence, tax home and closer connection tests) excludes Puerto Rico-source income from US federal income tax (IRC 933), so Puerto Rico is the one place where moving lowers US tax; a salary for work done in Puerto Rico is Puerto Rico-source, but US-source income is not covered, Social Security and Medicare (or self-employment) tax still apply, and US estate and gift tax continues to apply to mainland-born citizens.

succession.name: Puerto Rico
succession.summary: Puerto Rico has forced heirship: under the 2020 Civil Code half the estate is reserved for forced heirs, and the surviving spouse is now one of them. The other half is free. Puerto Rico has its own Trust Act (2012). The Hague Trusts Convention is not in force for the United States.
succession.reserved_share: Forced heirs hold the legítima of 1/2 of the estate (down from 2/3), the free portion is 1/2 (Civil Code 2020, Law 55-2020, arts. 1621 and 1623). The surviving spouse is a forced heir in the first order with descendants (art. 1720). Individual fractions were not read.
succession.foreign_law_note: No source read states how Puerto Rico's Civil Code 2020 treats the estate of a foreign national or whether the national law may be chosen.
succession.trust_note: HCCH shows the United States as signatory only, with no extension. Puerto Rico Trust Act (Law 219-2012) creates a registered trust as a separate estate; Act 153 of 30 July 2026 amends it (adds revocable trusts). No private-foundation statute was found, only non-profit entities.
open_questions: Effective date and content of Act 153 of 2026 not read.
Whether forced heirship reaches trust assets was not checked.
Private-foundation availability not confirmed.
Fractions per heir under the 2020 Code not read.
